articles.title: G20 trade meet exposes fault lines over global rules - The Hans India
articles.summary: G20 trade meet exposes fault lines over global rules  The Hans India
articles.full_text:
Milwaukee: A meeting of G20 trade ministers in Milwaukee has opened a wider debate over the future rules of global commerce, with the United States pressing major economies to reconsider long-established trade principles while seeking coordinated action against industrial overcapacity, forced labour and vulnerabilities in global supply chains.  
Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal is representing India at the two-day meeting hosted by United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, where differences over the World Trade Organization's Most-Favoured-Nation principle, tariffs, Chinese industrial capacity and government intervention in trade have emerged as key issues.  
The gathering is taking place at a time when the global trading system is increasingly divided between governments seeking to preserve WTO-centred multilateral rules and the Trump administration's emphasis on reciprocity, domestic manufacturing and the use of tariffs to address what Washington regards as unfair trading practices.  
The United States has placed four broad questions before ministers: eliminating forced labour from global supply chains, updating the Most-Favoured-Nation principle, opposing the weaponisation of food trade and confronting structural excess production capacity.  
Of these, the debate over Most-Favoured-Nation treatment could have the most far-reaching consequences.  
MFN is a central principle of the WTO system under which a trade advantage granted by one member to another generally has to be extended to other members. Washington argues that the existing system has failed to ensure reciprocity when countries maintain widely differing tariff structures and economic practices.  
India, however, arrived in Milwaukee emphasising its support for the multilateral trading system.  
The Commerce Ministry said India would work toward "a rules-based, open, inclusive, transparent, equitable and non-discriminatory multilateral trading system, with the World Trade Organization at its core, while ensuring adequate policy space for developing countries."  
The difference illustrates one of the fundamental questions confronting ministers in Milwaukee: whether problems in global trade should be addressed primarily through existing multilateral rules or through a greater emphasis on reciprocal treatment and coordinated action among like-minded economies.  
The first concrete outcome emerged Wednesday from steel.  
Members of the Global Forum on Steel Excess Capacity agreed on a new "Milwaukee Framework" designed to strengthen coordinated action against excess production.  
China, the world's largest steel producer, is not a member of the forum. Neither is India, the world's second-largest producer, making the distinction between the G20 meeting and the separate steel forum important.  
Asked whether participating countries had agreed to raise tariffs against Chinese steel, Greer said governments would determine their own measures.  
"Well, every country will do what they think is appropriate," he said. "We want to coordinate those measures. The United States has taken robust measures, and it probably makes sense for other countries to do that too."  
The steel debate is part of a larger dispute over industrial overcapacity and the role of state support in international competition.  
Washington and several other market economies have increasingly raised concerns about subsidies, below-market financing and production that exceeds domestic demand, particularly in China.  
The argument extends beyond steel to strategically important sectors including electric vehicles, batteries and clean-energy manufacturing.  
For emerging economies such as India, however, the debate also raises questions over how international trade rules distinguish between what advanced economies regard as market-distorting subsidies and industrial policies used by developing countries to build domestic manufacturing capacity.  
Forced labour is another major item on the Milwaukee agenda.  
The United States wants stronger international action to prevent goods produced with forced labour from entering global supply chains. While there is broad support for combating forced labour, questions remain over enforcement, traceability and the obligations imposed on importers to establish the origins of components and raw materials.  
Food trade could prove another sensitive area.  
Washington has called for G20 members to oppose the "weaponisation" of trade in food. The issue intersects with longstanding disagreements over agricultural export restrictions, food security and the policy space available to developing countries.  
India has traditionally defended flexibility for developing economies on food security and agriculture within the WTO system.  
Underlying all these discussions is a broader disagreement over tariffs.  
The Trump administration argues that trade policy should protect domestic manufacturing, strengthen supply chains and produce more reciprocal economic relationships.  
That philosophy was visible in the choice of Milwaukee as the venue.  
G20 ministers toured Rockwell Automation on Wednesday as the administration sought to showcase American manufacturing.  
Greer said the United States deliberately brought trade ministers to Milwaukee so they could see American factories and "see what we're trying to protect."  
But several countries attending the meeting have themselves faced US tariffs or trade pressure.  
Canada is among the countries navigating that tension.  
Canadian International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu is attending the ministerial, while Ottawa seeks to manage its economic relationship with Washington and diversify trade with other partners. Sidhu is also expected to meet India's representative Thursday.  
Brazil has meanwhile produced one of the first significant bilateral developments from Milwaukee.  
Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira and Minister of Development, Industry, Trade and Services Marcio Elias Rosa met Greer, with Brazil and the United States agreeing to establish a working group to discuss a possible trade agreement following tariff tensions between the two countries.  
The same Brazilian ministers also met Goyal as India pursued its own bilateral diplomacy on the sidelines.  
Goyal separately met Polish Finance and Economy Minister Andrzej Domański.  
"Discussed new avenues to further strengthen trade & investment ties, and how the India-EU FTA can create new opportunities for businesses and deepen economic cooperation between India & Poland," Goyal said after the meeting.  
The Commerce Minister also met Blake Moret, chairman and CEO of Rockwell Automation, and sought greater investment in India.  
"India's rapidly evolving manufacturing landscape, expanding industrial base, and strong technological capabilities present exciting avenues for collaboration in industrial automation and digital transformation," Goyal said.  
He invited Rockwell Automation "to leverage India's skilled engineering talent and supportive policy environment to build resilient, tech-driven supply chains for the world."  
For New Delhi, however, one of the most closely watched developments remains its trade negotiations with Washington.  
India and the United States are seeking to advance negotiations toward a bilateral trade agreement and an interim arrangement.  
The Commerce Ministry said before Goyal's visit that his US engagements would form part of efforts to advance "a balanced and mutually beneficial India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) and finalise an interim deal in line with the Joint Statement of 7 February 2026."  
The ministers therefore have two parallel tracks.  
Inside the formal sessions, governments are debating fundamental questions about WTO rules, reciprocity, industrial policy, supply chains and the role of tariffs.  
Outside them, ministers are pursuing bilateral trade agreements, investment opportunities and solutions to disputes that have become increasingly difficult to resolve through the multilateral system alone.  
The G20 Trade Ministers' Meeting continues Thursday, when further bilateral engagements are expected, and Greer is scheduled to hold a press conference.  
Attention will also turn to whether ministers can find common language on the most contentious issues, particularly Most-Favoured-Nation treatment, industrial overcapacity and food trade.  
The outcome could indicate whether the world's largest economies can still reach meaningful consensus on trade -- or whether international commerce is moving increasingly toward reciprocal arrangements, bilateral agreements and coalitions of countries sharing similar economic policies.

Brazil and India aim to expand Mercosur trade pact for broader market access
Milwaukee: Brazil and India are moving towards substantially expanding the existing India-Mercosur preferential trade agreement, with the two sides completing work on terms of reference that could pave the way for negotiations on a broader trade arrangement, a senior Brazilian minister has said.
Brazil’s Minister of Development, Industry, Trade and Services Márcio Elias Rosa said India was an important economic partner for Brazil and that the existing trade arrangement was too limited.
“India is a highly important trading partner to Brazil,” Rosa told IANS in response to a question on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministers’ Meeting here.
“India is an economy that is very important to the whole wide world. We have good relations with them,” he said.
Rosa was responding to questions from IANS after his meeting with India’s Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal.
“What we discussed now is a possibility of having an agreement, a broad agreement, between the two economies and Mercosur,” he said.
Mercosur is the South American trade bloc that includes Brazil.
Rosa said the existing preferential trade arrangement between India and Mercosur covered only a small number of products.
Expansion talks launched: India and Mercosur (Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia) announced on 14 September 2026 the start of negotiations to expand their existing Preferential Trade Agreement (PTA), aiming to deepen economic ties and create new opportunities for businesses on both sides.
Terms of Reference finalised: Both sides are finalising the Terms of Reference (ToR), which will define the scope and structure of the expanded agreement, with Brazil and India completing work on these terms as of 1 October 2026.
From PTA to FTA: The long-term goal is to upgrade the current PTA—operational since June 2009—into a comprehensive Free Trade Agreement (FTA) covering goods, services and investments, significantly enhancing market access and reducing trade barriers.
Current concessions: The existing PTA provides preferential tariff concessions on 450 tariff lines from India and 452 from Mercosur, with reductions ranging from 10% to 100%.
Paperless trade protocol: On 14 September, India and Mercosur signed the First Additional Protocol to the PTA, facilitating the acceptance of electronic Certificates of Origin (CoO) to streamline customs procedures and support paperless trade.
Strategic diversification: The move aligns with India’s strategy to diversify export markets amid global economic volatility and supports Brazil’s push to broaden commercial relationships beyond existing tariff preferences.
Trade target: During Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s visit to India in February 2026, both countries agreed to double bilateral trade to US$30 billion by 2030, providing a backdrop for the expanded negotiations.
“We already have a tariff preference agreement, but it’s very shy. It’s just 450 tariff funds. Meaning that nothing absolutely. So we need to expand that,” he said, according to the English interpretation provided during the gaggle.

The India-US trade agreement is in the "short strokes" of negotiations, but the deal is not yet imminent. United States Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer has indicated that discussions between the two sides are continuing over unresolved issues. He added that PM Modi and US President Donald Trump could speak again soon to review the progress of the negotiations.
The US trade chief added that the two sides have identified the full set of items that were still proving to be sticking points and were working towards resolving them.
Commenting on the negotiations, the Greer said, "We had a very constructive conversation with Minister Piyush Goyal... We are continually trying to finish the trade deal with India, we are in the short strokes. I think we are towards the end of it. President Trump and the Prime Minister Modi had a constructive call yesterday morning. At the same time, I don't think there is something imminent.”
He added, “But we truly have identified the universe of items that are sticking points, and we are working diligently toward them. The President and the Prime Minister may have another call very soon on this just to assess progress and where we are."
Goyal, Greer hold talks in Milwaukee
The latest comments came after Union commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal held talks with Greer on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministers' Meeting in Milwaukee. The meeting was part of ongoing bilateral efforts to conclude a "balanced and mutually beneficial" trade agreement between New Delhi and Washington.
Goyal had earlier said that the discussions were aimed at an early conclusion of an interim agreement under the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA).
In a post on X, he wrote, "Met USTR Jamieson Greer, US trade representative, on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministers' Meeting in Milwaukee. Had a productive discussion with USTR Greer towards early conclusion of a mutually beneficial interim agreement under the India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement. We also exchanged views on G20 deliberations under US Chairship."
The talks between Goyal and Greer took place on Wednesday, the same day PM Modi and Trump held a telephone conversation. The two leaders discussed progress in trade, defence, energy, critical technologies and other areas of mutual interest.
What's after February framework?
Ahead of Goyal's visit, the ministry said his discussions with the US counterpart would focus on advancing the Bilateral Trade Agreement and finalising an interim deal in line with the Joint Statement of February 7, 2026.
"Goyal will also engage bilaterally with his counterpart from the United States as part of ongoing efforts to advance a balanced and mutually beneficial India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) and finalise an interim deal in line with the Joint Statement of 7 February 2026."
India and the US had announced in February this year that they had finalised the framework for the initial phase of the Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA). However, negotiations continued following changes in the US tariff landscape.
Goyal had said on September 24 that the India-US trade pact was "done and dusted", but added that it would be executed once the US gives India the right competitive advantage over its competitors in the American market.

Speaking at the 2026 G20 Trade Ministers Meeting in Milwaukee on the India-Canada trade deal, Sidhu said, "The vision that leaders have set out for us is to scale trade from USD 30 billion to USD 70 billion within the next five years. How do we get there? Part of it is through the greater facilitation of free trade. Right now, negotiations are ongoing to see what we can do together to build our economies in a complementary manner rather than competing with one another."

Highlighting the recent momentum in talks, the Canadian minister noted that the fifth round of negotiations for the trade agreement is scheduled to take place in Ottawa on Monday.
"I was just in India about 10 days ago, meeting with Minister Piyush Goyal in Mumbai. We were discussing Round 4 then. Round 5 will happen in Ottawa on Monday, and we are going to continue those conversations. Of course, negotiations are always tough, but we look forward to concluding in the coming months. It is important that Canada continues to have these conversations. Prime Minister Carney and Prime Minister Modi have had excellent conversations on how we can bring our economies closer together,' Sidhu said.
"Well, negotiations are ongoing, so I will be very careful about detailing that through the media. However, you can tell from my conversations that it is about collaboration. India is looking to diversify some of its supply chains. If you look at critical minerals, India has a growing auto sector, and for EVs and batteries, Canada is the only country in the Western Hemisphere that has every single element to make an electro-paddock. And so there is something that we can add. We just held our investment summit in Toronto. We had a lot of amazing investors come to Canada... We came out with about $500 million in commitments. So we have a lot of projects that we can work on together, energy, critical minerals, aerospace, and others," he added.
Also Read: India, Canada to hold next round of talks from October 5 for proposed trade pact: Piyush Goyal
Earlier, Union Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said that India and Canada have agreed to fast-track negotiations for a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), with the next round of talks scheduled to begin on October 5.
Goyal said he had concluded the fourth round of negotiations for the proposed trade agreement with his Canadian counterpart, Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu, in Mumbai last week.
"I have concluded the fourth round of negotiations for the Canada trade deal with my counterpart, Mr Maninder Sidhu in Mumbai on Friday. Very productive discussions, and both sides have resolved to fast-track negotiations, in view of which our team is now slated to go for the fifth round. Fifth of October. So you can see that as the progress is taking shape, the speed of negotiations with Canada is also improving. Let's see, the next 90 days should be a very defining period in the Canada-India relationship," he said.
The latest round follows a renewed push by the two countries to conclude a comprehensive trade agreement. Canada had said ahead of Sidhu's September 18-19 visit to Mumbai that three rounds of the fresh CEPA negotiations had been completed and that both sides shared the objective of concluding negotiations by the end of 2026.
India and Canada have discussed a comprehensive trade pact for more than a decade. Negotiations were formally relaunched in March 2022, with the two sides also pursuing an Early Progress Trade Agreement as an interim step. Nine negotiating rounds were held between 2022 and 2023 before the process was paused in August 2023 amid a period of strain in bilateral relations.
Trade engagement gathered momentum again in 2025. The two countries subsequently launched a fresh CEPA process, with Goyal and Sidhu signing the Terms of Reference on March 2, 2026, during Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to India.
Both governments committed to seeking conclusion of the negotiations by the end of 2026.
Bilateral trade between India and Canada stood at around USD 8 billion in FY 2025-26, with India exporting goods worth USD 4.67 billion and importing USD 3.28 billion, according to the Commerce Ministry.

articles.title: Woman's heartbreaking take on life as parents remain missing after Nepal floods - India Today
articles.summary: Woman's heartbreaking take on life as parents remain missing after Nepal floods  India TodayIn Flood-Hit Nepal, Teachers Mourn Students Who Never Returned  NDTVNepal floods threaten jobs and livelihoods beyond disaster zone: ILO  UN NewsThe Sunita Narain Show: What led to the Himalayan tragedy in Nepal?  downtoearth.org.in‘I do not know if the doctor survived’: young mothers recall ‘living hell’ of Nepal’s floods  theguardian.com
articles.full_text:
Tanvi's YouTube video came more than a month after her parents went missing while on the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra. They have remained untraceable since flash floods struck near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26.
A young woman, whose parents went missing during the devastating Nepal flash floods, broke down in a heartbreaking video as she spoke about the uncertainty surrounding their disappearance and the challenges she has been facing in life in the past one month.
Tanvi’s YouTube video came more than a month after her parents went missing while on the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra. They have remained untraceable since flash floods struck near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastating towns and villages across northern and central Nepal.
In the video titled “I haven't really talked about this...30 days since Nepal,” Tanvi spoke through tears about her parents, Venkatram and Anagha Annamdevara, who were part of a 67-member pilgrimage group caught in the disaster.
As she struggled to come to terms with their absence, Tanvi recalled the little things around her home that constantly reminded her of her parents. She also questioned why they had to face such a tragedy when they were still so young, with their lives ahead of them.
“It has been 30 days since the Nepal floods. My parents went on the Kailash Yatra on August 26. They were at the immigration centre, which was the worst-hit location during the Nepal floods,” she said in the video posted on September 26, repeatedly wiping away her tears.
Tanvi said the past month had been consumed by legal formalities, financial responsibilities and the daunting task of managing everything her parents had built. Amid the paperwork and practical demands of the crisis, she admitted that she had barely processed the emotional reality of their absence.
“I haven't even processed it at all. For the past 30 days, I have been running around, taking care of all the legal and financial work and trying to maintain everything my parents have,” she said.
Looking around her home, she recalled the little things that reminded her of her parents. A water bottle bought by her mother, a speaker bought by her father and countless other everyday objects had become reminders of the people she was desperately hoping to see again.
“My parents have made me disgustingly educated and privileged because I have just realised how much I have around me. My mom bought this bottle, and my dad bought the speaker. They worked so hard, for what? For them to leave?” she said.
Her grief was intertwined with anger and disbelief. At 52 and 49, respectively, her parents were still young and had only just reached a stage in life when they could begin enjoying the rewards of years of hard work.
“They were so young. They were supposed to start enjoying their lives now. They were supposed to start travelling. And the first trip was the Kailash Yatra. I am just angry at the world, at the universe. I don't understand. Why them?” she said.
For a while, Tanvi had convinced herself that her parents would return. They were originally expected home on September 6, but she continued to hold on to hope even after that date passed.
“I was delusional enough to wait until September 15, thinking they were going to come back. Reality hit me late, and I realised that maybe they weren't going to come back,” she said.
As per previous social media posts, her parents were part of a 67-member Kailash Yatra group. Tanvi said she had been unable to establish contact with either the group or the organisation handling the pilgrimage. Their last known location was around the immigration centre and the Friendship Bridge in Nepal.
Her parents' disappearance also coincided with a crucial milestone in Tanvi's own life. On August 30, she was scheduled to appear for the NEET PG examination, an important step in her journey towards becoming a doctor. Despite the uncertainty and fear surrounding her parents' whereabouts, she went to the examination centre and sat for the test.
Looking back at the past month, Tanvi said much of what she had been doing was driven by the desire to make her parents proud. Taking responsibility for their affairs had made her realise just how much they had done for her.
“For the past 30 days, everything I have been doing has been solely to make my parents proud. I am just trying to protect everything my parents worked so hard for,” she said.
She also spoke fondly of her mother, describing her as the happiest person she knew. Her mother loved dressing up, taking pictures and bringing joy to those around her. For Tanvi, preserving her parents' memories has become an important part of navigating the uncertainty.
“I can never let these things go because I can never let my parents go. I have to always remember them and make sure everybody remembers them because they were such great people,” she said.
Beyond sharing her own ordeal, Tanvi used the video to reflect on the unpredictability of life and the importance of relationships. She urged people to spend more time with their parents, let go of grudges and build relationships where children feel comfortable discussing even difficult subjects.
“I want every parent to be transparent with their children about their bank accounts and financial situations. More than that, you need to be a friend to your child,” she said.
She also spoke about how a major personal tragedy can change one's perspective on everyday problems, making many of the things that once seemed significant feel inconsequential.
“When you experience a loss, especially the loss of a parent, you realise that everything else doesn't even matter,” she said.
In the video caption, Tanvi acknowledged the many emotions she had experienced over the past month, including fear, hope, anger, helplessness, exhaustion, guilt and gratitude.
There was much happening behind the updates she had been sharing online that people could not see. She wanted to document how she was feeling without pretending that everything was fine.
“I didn't make this video with a script or a plan. I just wanted to sit down and talk honestly, openly and without trying to make everything sound okay,” she wrote.
Tanvi also thanked everyone who had checked in, shared information, prayed, offered help or continued asking for updates, adding that the support meant more to her and her family than she could express.
“Please keep my parents, Anagha and Venkatram, in your thoughts,” she concluded.
Over a month after the disaster, at least 1,453 people had died and 5,285 remained unaccounted for, data from Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) showed. The agency also said that 13,795 people had been rescued.

articles.summary: 'Message of hope': California becomes 18th US state to ban child marriage  The Times of IndiaCalifornia bans child marriage, a practice still legal in 32 US states  bbc.comNo More Child Brides In California, Governor Newsom Ends Practice Still Legal In 32 States  NDTVGovernor Newsom signs bill to ban child marriage  California State Portal | CA.govCalifornia bans child marriage: These 32 US states still allow minors to marry; 2 have no minimum age &nb...

California has officially banned child marriage after Governor Gavin Newsom signed legislation setting 18 as the minimum age for marriage and domestic partnerships in the state.
Assembly Bill 1267, authored by Democratic Assemblywoman Gail Pellerin of Santa Cruz, repeals provisions that previously allowed minors to marry with parental consent and court approval. The law will come into effect on January 1, 2027.
California ends exceptions for minors
Newsom signed the legislation on Wednesday alongside media personality and child marriage survivor Courtney Stodden, who was allowed by her parents to marry actor Doug Hutchison when she was 16 and he was 51.
“This is a long overdue measure to protect young Californians and minors. Today, California kids are safer than ever before,” Newsom said, according to NBC Los Angeles.
The legislation was sponsored by Unchained at Last and the California Commission on the Status of Women and Girls. California had previously been among the US states without a statutory minimum marriage age.
Under the earlier law, minors could marry if they had parental consent and court approval. 
The law also provided no mechanism for people under 18 to obtain a divorce.
Survivors welcome new law
Stodden, who has campaigned against child marriage, described the legislation as a “victory” and said she would continue campaigning until children were protected from marriage across all 50 states.
“Governor Newsom's action today made clear to me and to survivors of child marriage everywhere that we should never have been expected to carry this burden,” Stodden said, according to NBC Los Angeles.
She also spoke about feelings of guilt associated with her experience.
“Today really taught me something. It taught me that what happened to me and to these other girls was wrong. And I was never the problem,” Stodden told NBC Los Angeles.
Other survivors also welcomed the legislation. Brittany Bee, who told the BBC she was married at 17 after trying to escape an abusive home, said, “California has sent a clear message to the world today. A message of hope for all children that they may be free from systemic violence. That they may choose their own path.”
How common was child marriage in California?
Global Hope 365 said around 35,000 marriages involving minors took place in California between 2000 and 2021, with most involving an underage girl and an adult man, according to NBC Los Angeles.
Advocacy group Unchained At Last estimated that about 9,000 girls were married each year in California and said almost all child marriages involved girls marrying adult men.
Rima Nashashibi, founder and president of Global Hope 365 and founder of the California Coalition to End Child Marriage, said survivors had been central to the campaign for a ban.
“The heart of this effort has always been the survivors,” Pellerin said. “They told us what it means to be a child in a marriage you did not freely choose.”
California becomes 18th US state to ban child marriage
California is the 18th US state to completely ban child marriage since 2018. The practice remains legal in 32 states, although some have set minimum ages below 18 under specific conditions.
Mississippi and New Mexico do not have a statutory minimum age, while other states permit marriage below 18 in certain circumstances.
Stodden said she now wanted to focus on Nevada, where she was married at 16. “After I got married in Nevada, they upped it to 17, but that's not good enough for me,” she said.
The new California law will take effect on January 1, 2027, after which people must be at least 18 to marry in the state.

According to a Wall Street Journal (WDJ) report, the discussion took place on September 29 after nearly two dozen CEOs met Trump for lunch and agreed to a set of voluntary principles for safer AI development. During the luncheon, tech executives including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reportedly asked Dario Amodei why he was being so extreme in public about AI capabilities and the risks they could create. Amodei defended his position, saying it was important to be honest with the public and not play down the risks.

Why Jensen Huang questioned Dario Amodei
The private discussion highlights a growing difference among major AI companies over how quickly the technology should develop and how much attention should be given to its risks.
Dario Amodei has repeatedly warned about the possible dangers of advanced AI, including cyberattacks and large-scale job losses. 
He has also criticised the White House and some technology companies for playing down those risks.
At Tuesday's meeting, Amodei told other executives that the public should be given an accurate picture of what AI models can do and the risks they pose, according to people familiar with the discussion cited by the WSJ.
Tech CEOs agree to safety principles
Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson brought the AI executives together as pressure grows over the safety of increasingly capable AI systems. The companies agreed to work with independent auditors and establish stronger internal controls to check whether their AI systems operate as intended. They also agreed to work to prevent AI tools from hacking or accessing technical systems in unintended ways.

Top technology executives have signed an agreement with US President Donald Trump promising stronger safeguards for increasingly powerful artificial intelligence systems. But despite the document being signed by some of the biggest names in the tech industry, a basic spelling mistake in Trump's title went unnoticed, which drew widespread mockery online.
The document, titled the "White House Accord on Super Intelligence", identifies Trump as the "President of the Unites States", instead of the "United States".
The typo appears beneath Trump's prominent signature on the second page of the accord, which was circulated publicly by the White House and later shared by Trump on his Truth Social account.
Trump signed the agreement on Tuesday after hosting several technology leaders at the White House. The signatories included Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI president Greg Brockman, xAI CEO Elon Musk and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
Sundar Pichai shares accord online, also appears to miss typo
Pichai also shared the document on X, saying Google had invested hundreds of billions of dollars in the US and was committed to working with other industry leaders to establish norms and build public confidence around AI.
However, the typo in the document appeared to have gone unnoticed by Pichai and the other signatories before it was published.
The error quickly became a talking point online, with users sharing screenshots of the document and highlighting the words "Unites States".
One user wrote: "What about the typo!! Super intelligence doesn’t pick up the super intelligent typo?"
Another mocked the agreement by saying: "Super Intelligence is AI without spell check."
A third user pointed to the purpose of the agreement, asking whether a typo missed by the people overseeing "super intelligence" raised questions about what else could potentially be overlooked.
The spelling error drew particular attention because the agreement itself focuses on safeguards and oversight for advanced AI systems.
What does Trump's AI accord say?
The voluntary agreement calls on participating AI companies to introduce several layers of safeguards around their systems.
These include internal monitoring of model capabilities, an internal oversight team, independent external audits and a board-level committee responsible for receiving reports and ensuring that identified problems are addressed.
Trump has described the accord as "morally binding", although it is not legally enforceable. The document also says that some of the measures could eventually be turned into laws or regulations.
The agreement comes as AI development and the potential risks posed by increasingly capable systems have become a major focus of debate in the US.
Trump has also promoted the term "super intelligence" as his preferred description for AI. On Tuesday, he signed an executive order directing the federal government to replace references to "artificial intelligence" and "AI" with "super intelligence" or "SI".
The White House had not immediately commented on the spelling error or said whether a corrected version of the accord would be issued.

The ties between India and China are “better” today as compared to a couple of years ago, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has said, underlining that as the border issues are resolved, the relationship returns to normalcy.
Jaishankar was responding to a question on India-China relations, which have seen an upswing in recent times, including with President Xi Jinping’s recent visit to India for the BRICS Leaders’ Summit hosted by New Delhi.
“If you asked me, compared to where you were in 2025, is the relationship better today? I would say yes. Compared to 2024, even more so,” Jaishankar said during a conversation hosted at Asia Society. He said it’s not so much a “structural change”, but part of the reason why things have improved is “they had gone so much off-track that the moment you stabilised it, it was going to improve, because after what happened in 2020 and the long standoff that we had on the border, the relationship had really been impacted.”
Following the 2020 border standoff between India and China, all “normal contacts” between the two nations had come to a halt, he said, adding that while “trade was continuing”, official exchanges, visa issuance, and flights had been impacted.
“So once the border standoff was resolved, it was natural that this would start to improve,” he said.
There was also this logic, which Delhi had long been conveying to Beijing, that a “standoff between us, a dip in our relationship, actually doesn’t help either of us. In fact, it is third parties who will take advantage of that.
“We also maintained consistently a very elementary principle of statecraft - don’t get locked into a problem which benefits others,” Jaishankar said. “It took a little while for the Chinese side to agree with that, for whatever reason, but I don’t think that long standoff served our interests. It certainly didn’t serve theirs. And to the extent there is an improvement in our relations, I think it certainly helps our position,” not only vis-a-vis China but vis-a-vis the rest of the world, he said. “Because I don’t want to get totally focused to my disadvantage on one particular relationship and issue. If I can find a solution which works for me, I would rather do that,” he said.
“We came down to a very fundamental principle, which is that the state of the border determines the state of the relationship.
You can’t have tension...on the border and say the relationship should be normal. So what we’ve had is, as the border comes back more towards normalcy, the relationship comes back more towards normalcy, and if the relationship comes back more towards normalcy, it helps both of us,” Jaishankar said.

Putin said Russia would use all weapons at its disposal if Kaliningrad or other territory came under direct attack. The warning, delivered amid tensions over Ukraine, drew a Nato response that nuclear threats were unhelpful.
Moscow has made clear it would defend Kaliningrad with nuclear weapons if necessary, Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday, warning the West against escalating tensions over Ukraine.
Speaking at the Valdai Forum in Moscow, Putin said Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to coexist peacefully, but stressed that Moscow would use all weapons in its arsenal if Kaliningrad or other Russian territory came under direct attack.
"If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation — in this case, we are referring to Kaliningrad, and perhaps other territories as well — the question of the Russian Federation deploying all the weapons at our country's disposal will, of course, inevitably and immediately be on the agenda," Putin said.
"This is inevitable," he added.
Kaliningrad, Russia's westernmost territory, is located between Nato members Poland and Lithuania and is heavily militarised. Putin said Russia understood that Nato was "twice our size" and would have to rely on its military advantages in any confrontation.
He also pointed to the nuclear capabilities of France and Britain, saying Russia was fully aware of them but maintained that Moscow possessed weapons that gave it a "competitive advantage".
Putin's remarks came after Nato said it had received a diplomatic note from Moscow warning that Russia was prepared to use nuclear weapons if the alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance had responded by stressing that it was defensive in nature and that nuclear threats were unhelpful.
Relations between Russia and the West have remained deeply strained since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. European governments have also accused Russia of intensifying what they describe as a "hybrid war" involving alleged sabotage and arson. Moscow denies the accusations and rejects claims that it is preparing to attack a Nato country.
Putin warned that continued escalation could eventually reach a point from which there would be no return.
"We must realise that the moment when nothing can be changed any longer may come very quickly and unexpectedly for everyone," he said, warning that increasingly severe retaliatory measures could lead to "a fatal point of no return".
He said the world's leading powers possessed weapons capable of causing catastrophic destruction and urged governments to avoid a situation in which such weapons could be used.
Putin also said he was ready for a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump if a proper agenda was agreed in advance.
On Ukraine, Putin ruled out halting Russian strikes against Ukrainian targets in the Black Sea region. He acknowledged that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries had cost Russia about 1% of its GDP and said Moscow was responding in kind.
While warning of the potential consequences of Western support for Ukrainian deep strikes inside Russia, Putin said Moscow was not planning to attack European arms factories supplying Ukraine "tomorrow".

articles.title: India’s inflation shock adds pressure on central bank - The Real Economy Blog
articles.summary: India’s inflation shock adds pressure on central bank  The Real Economy Blog
articles.full_text:
The Reserve Bank of India is likely to raise its policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% at its October 5-7 meeting, as inflation has moved above target and price pressures are broadening while economic activity remains resilient.
The case for a hike has strengthened considerably since the RBI’s August meeting.
Headline CPI inflation accelerated to 4.82% in August from 4.45% in July, moving above the central bank’s 4% target for a third consecutive month.

Food inflation rose to 5.95%, while core inflation also increased to 4.2% from 3.86% in July. Importantly, price pressures have broadened beyond food and fuel, suggesting the increase is becoming less concentrated in a handful of volatile categories.
Wholesale inflation provides another indication. Overall WPI inflation increased to 9.92% from 9.78% in July. At the same time, the gap between wholesale and consumer inflation narrowed to roughly 5.1 percentage points from 5.3 percentage points.
That narrowing was driven primarily by consumer inflation moving higher rather than a decline in wholesale inflation. Producer prices remain elevated while consumer prices are beginning to catch up.
The external policy environment has also shifted.
Major central banks have moved toward tighter policy as the energy shock has pushed inflation higher, while global bond yields have risen as investors reassess how persistent inflation will be.
For India, the issue is not simply whether the RBI should match the actions of other central banks. It is the effect of global interest rates on the interest-rate differential, capital flows and the rupee.
As yields on U.S. and other developed-market securities rise, Indian assets can become relatively less attractive at the margin. A narrower yield differential can put pressure on portfolio flows and the exchange rate. That can put pressure on capital flows and the rupee, raising the domestic cost of imported commodities and adding to inflationary pressure.
The growth data gives the RBI room to tighten.
Real GDP growth accelerated to 7.8% year-on-year in the April-June quarter of 2026-27, well above the RBI’s 7.0% projection.
High-frequency indicators point in the same direction. Industrial production accelerated to 8.0% year-on-year in August, from 6.7% in July. While manufacturing PMI rose to 55.1 from 52.8 in August, its highest level in seven months.
The combination of resilient domestic demand and broadening inflation gives the RBI an opportunity to address the inflation shock before it becomes more deeply embedded in the economy.
We expect the RBI to raise the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% at its next meeting, while emphasizing that subsequent moves will remain dependent on the evolution of inflation and the energy shock.
The hike should be viewed less as a response to an overheating economy and more as an effort to prevent a temporary external price shock from becoming embedded in domestic inflation expectations.

Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday warned that the world was living through a dangerous moment, saying escalating international conflicts could reach a “fatal point of no return” and stressing that weapons of mass destruction must never be used.
Speaking at the Valdai Forum of international Russia experts in Moscow, Putin said the world’s leading powers possessed arsenals capable of destroying all life or reducing the Earth to a “catastrophic state”.
He urged countries to recognise how quickly escalating retaliation could lead to an irreversible situation.
“We must realise that the moment when nothing can be changed any longer may come very quickly and unexpectedly for everyone. The logic of escalating, increasingly harsh retaliatory measures leads to a fatal point of no return,” Putin said.
“At the heart of this escalation lie arrogance and overconfidence. This is a path to the brink of the abyss. All the more so today, when the arsenals of the world’s leading powers contain weapons capable of destroying all life or, at the very least, reducing the Earth to a catastrophic state. Can we be certain that these weapons will never be used? Well, of course not. 
We must bear this in mind and avoid such an outcome.”
Putin warns of Western role in Ukraine conflict
Putin said Ukraine would not be able to carry out attacks deep inside Russia without Western technical support, arguing that such assistance amounted to direct involvement in the conflict.
He said Russia viewed attempts to use Ukraine as a proxy to fight Russia as a threat. Putin also said Moscow was not planning to attack factories in other countries that manufacture weapons for Ukraine, but warned that Russia's military and intelligence services needed to closely monitor them.
“We are not going to attack tomorrow enterprises in countries which supply weapons to Ukraine, but that's a threat,” Putin said.
Putin also said Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries had cost Russia 1% of its gross domestic product.
He said Ukraine had “partially achieved its objectives” through the attacks, but added that Russia was responding in kind.
He further said Ukraine had damaged more than 100 Russian vessels in the Black Sea and that Moscow was now responding.
Russia issues warning over Kaliningrad
Putin said Russia would consider using the full range of weapons in its arsenal if its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad came under threat. He maintained that Russia did not plan to attack anyone but would respond to aggression.
“We are not going to attack anyone, but will respond if we face aggression,” Putin said.
Kaliningrad is a Russian territory on the Baltic Sea separated from mainland Russia by other countries and located between Nato members Poland and Lithuania. The region has become a focus of tensions between Moscow and the alliance.
In a separate development on Thursday, the Kremlin said Russia's recent letter to Nato on Kaliningrad should not be viewed as confrontational. The document accused the alliance of pursuing a “dangerous and reckless course” carrying “high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict”.
Putin also said Russia was not threatening European countries and did not plan to attack them.
“We are not threatening anyone and we do not plan to attack any European countries, not in 2030, not in 2050,” he said.
Putin says global conflicts likely to continue
Putin said international conflicts were likely to continue as the global order undergoes fundamental changes, although he said the situation would improve as what he described as Western hegemony waned.
“Regardless of which scenario unfolds globally in the coming years, the continuation of international conflicts is, unfortunately, highly likely. This is due in part to the fact that ongoing fundamental shifts—and the opportunities they present—fuel ambitions and a willingness to take risks for the sake of a seemingly massive payoff,” Putin said.
He again stressed the need to avoid catastrophic scenarios.
Putin also said Russia supported a possible trilateral meeting with Chinese President 
Xi Jinping
 and US President Donald Trump, although he said an agenda for such talks would first need to be worked out.
On the Middle East, Putin said he hoped the Strait of Hormuz would remain open to shipping and that sanctions on Iran would be lifted. He also said Russia's proposals to deliver enriched uranium from Iran to Russia remained valid.
Putin said Russia remained interested in cooperation with Japan but was concerned about what he described as the country's militarisation.
He added that Japanese companies continued to operate in Russia and that Moscow supported them and others working with Russia.
He also criticised military drills and arrests of Russian vessels as forms of escalation and said Russia had a competitive advantage in defending itself.

articles.title: Trump–Xi Thaw And What It Will Mean For India And America Ties - Free Press Journal
articles.summary: Trump–Xi Thaw And What It Will Mean For India And America Ties  Free Press Journal
articles.full_text:
As Washington and Beijing explore a new framework for managing rivalry, India must prepare for a world in which American strategic priorities may no longer automatically align with its own.
Geopolitics is rarely short of ironies. The man who built his political identity around confronting China is now rolling out the red carpet for its president. Donald Trump’s personal reception of Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews, complete with military honours—a 21-gun salute and a fighter-aircraft flypast—captured a striking moment in the changing world order. The two countries that appeared locked in an escalating confrontation are now exploring how to compete without allowing rivalry to spiral out of control.
The spectacle was more than diplomatic choreography. It reflected a hard reality: neither superpower can easily bend the other to its will. America retains formidable military, technological, and financial advantages, but China has demonstrated its capacity to withstand economic pressure. Their engagement is, therefore, not necessarily reconciliation; it is an attempt to establish the terms of coexistence.
For India, the implications extend well beyond a presidential handshake. New Delhi must prepare for a world in which Washington can deepen its partnership with India while negotiating accommodations with Beijing. The assumption that an enduring American confrontation with China will automatically serve Indian interests is no longer a safe foundation for foreign policy.
Why Trump Chose Pragmatism
Trump’s approach to China combines coercion with transactional bargaining. His second-term diplomacy suggests that tariffs and economic pressure, while useful instruments of leverage, cannot secure every American objective.
Prolonged confrontation carries costs. Trade uncertainty disrupts businesses, complicates supply chains, and threatens American exporters. China’s position in critical minerals further complicates Washington’s calculations. The need to manage other international crises, including Iran, provides another incentive to prevent the China relationship from becoming an uncontrollable front.
Trump’s engagement offers potential economic gains: greater Chinese purchases of American agricultural products, energy supplies and industrial goods, improved access to critical minerals, and opportunities for American businesses. Cooperation on fentanyl-related chemicals and artificial intelligence could also address specific security concerns.
Yet, a temporary trade truce is not a permanent settlement. Technology restrictions, Taiwan, and Iran remain contentious. The real test is whether diplomatic warmth produces enforceable commitments benefiting American workers, businesses, and national security. Trump’s approach is better understood as transactional management than as an end to strategic competition.
China Seeks Competitive Coexistence
Beijing, too, has reasons to welcome a less confrontational atmosphere. Its message is that China should be treated as a major power entitled to compete on its own terms.
The emerging Chinese formula—cooperation where possible, competition within limits, and differences managed through dialogue—reflects an effort to make rivalry predictable. Washington and Beijing need not become friends to avoid becoming enemies.
China increasingly believes American pressure can impose costs but cannot easily compel it to change its fundamental policies. This confidence should not be mistaken for the disappearance of American advantages. The United States retains powerful alliances, advanced research institutions, financial influence, and substantial military capabilities.
The summit nevertheless suggests that trade, technology, and artificial intelligence may become subjects of negotiation alongside confrontation.
Taiwan remains the most dangerous fault line. Beijing regards it as a core national interest, while American arms sales and support for Taipei remain contentious. Neither ceremonial warmth nor economic accommodation resolves this fundamental disagreement. A crisis over Taiwan could overwhelm the carefully cultivated atmosphere.
Ripples Across Asia And West Asia
Across Asia, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and Southeast Asian countries will watch how Washington balances deterrence with accommodation. Reduced tensions could lower the immediate danger of military confrontation and improve regional economic stability. But they could also give Beijing additional diplomatic space to expand its influence.
For India, the concern is whether Washington’s changing calculations affect the strategic foundations of the Indo-Pacific. The Quad and partnerships with America, Japan, and Australia remain relevant. However, their value cannot rest solely on the expectation of uninterrupted US-China confrontation.
The implications extend to West Asia. America remains central to Gulf security, while China has developed extensive economic relationships across the region. Beijing’s ability to maintain channels with countries Washington confronts gives it diplomatic room for manoeuvre without direct military entanglement.
India has vital interests here—energy supplies, trade, investment, and millions of Indians working in the Gulf. New Delhi must preserve constructive relations with Washington, Beijing, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Iran, and other regional powers. Its objective should be to prevent great-power rivalry from undermining Indian interests.
Five Challenges For India
The first is economic. If American businesses regain confidence in Chinese markets, India could face intensified competition for manufacturing investment. New Delhi must improve infrastructure, regulatory predictability, and business conditions to attract companies seeking alternatives to China.
The second is technological. Artificial intelligence, advanced computing, batteries, and critical minerals are increasingly central to national power. If Washington and Beijing shape global technology rules, India must ensure its interests are represented while strengthening domestic research and innovation.
The third is security. The unresolved boundary dispute with China demands military preparedness, infrastructure development, and diplomatic engagement. An American accommodation with Beijing cannot create complacency in New Delhi.
The fourth concerns Pakistan. China’s strategic partnership with Islamabad remains an important element of India’s security environment. New Delhi must assess developments on its Northern and Western fronts independently of changes in US-China relations.
The fifth is diplomatic. India must deepen cooperation with America without becoming dependent on Washington. Defence partnerships and advanced technology are valuable, but they cannot substitute for independent judgement on Russia, Iran, and other international issues.
Strength At Home, Autonomy Abroad
India’s response should be neither anxiety over American accommodation nor complacency about Chinese ambitions. It must enlarge its own room for manoeuvre.
New Delhi should deepen defence and technological cooperation with Washington while strengthening partnerships with Japan, Australia, Europe, and Southeast Asia. A competitive manufacturing base, stronger domestic defence industry, secure supply chains, and investment in emerging technologies will enhance its bargaining power.
Equally, India should maintain communication with Beijing. Managing competition does not mean abandoning legitimate security concerns, just as defending national interests does not require treating every diplomatic engagement as a concession.
The Trump-Xi summit has not dismantled the rivalry between America and China; it has demonstrated that even fierce competitors may seek accommodation when confrontation becomes too costly.
For India, the lesson is clear: international relationships are never permanently fixed. Yesterday’s adversaries can negotiate tomorrow’s arrangements. India must remain engaged with America, manage its difficult relationship with China, and strengthen partnerships across Asia and the Global South.
In a world where rivals can embrace when interests converge, India’s ultimate insurance lies not in the permanence of another country’s hostility towards China, but in the strength of its own national power.
The writer is a senior political analyst and strategic affairs columnist based in Shimla.

Americans are turning against Donald Trump's handling of economy, pri  The Times of IndiaMost blame President Trump for higher prices and are unhappy with how he is handling the economy  AP-NORCMost Americans blame Trump for high prices as his economic approval hits new low, AP-NORC poll shows  AP News8 in 10 Americans disapprove of Trump on inflation. That’s extremely rare for a president  CNNWarning signs multiply for ...
articles.full_text:
Americans are increasingly unhappy with President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy and rising prices, with a new poll showing a sharp drop in his economic approval and a majority blaming his policies for persistently high costs.
Only 17% of US adults approve of Trump’s handling of the cost of living, while just 26% approve of his handling of the economy, according to an Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll.
The economic approval figure is a new low and is down 14 percentage points from March 2025, shortly after Trump began his second term.
The poll also found that 65% of Americans blame Trump’s policies more than factors outside his control for continued high prices.
The findings come weeks before the midterm elections, with Republicans seeking to retain control of Congress and Trump campaigning at rallies across the country.
Rising costs weigh on Trump’s economic record
Americans have become increasingly concerned about paying for essentials such as food and petrol. Around half of US adults said they were “extremely” or “very” concerned about being able to fill their petrol tanks, up from 39% in July. A similar share expressed high concern about affording food.
“I was hoping it would be better or different, but it’s not really good," Robert Gault, 66, a retired factory worker from Pennsylvania who describes himself as a Republican, told news agency AP.
“Our president, I thought, was going to help the country, and so far he has not really seemed to have done that with the economy or in general. He’s not really done what I was hoping he would," Gault said. “He said, 'Make America Great Again.' And I have not seen him do that.”
Pedro Sanchez, 52, a Trump voter who works in law enforcement in California, said rising fuel costs had reduced his disposable income.
“Prices are ‘extremely exorbitant. Just the cost of everything is going up as a result of fuel,” Sanchez said, according to AP. “I used to have a lot more disposable income. I don’t have that any more. It’s gotten eaten up because of all these increases in the cost of everything.”
About seven in 10 Americans said Trump’s handling of the cost of living had been “worse than expected”. Around six in 10 Republicans also disapproved of his performance on the issue, up from about half in April.
Bethany Lnenicka, 41, a small-farm operator from Iowa and a political independent who typically votes Republican, said she had expected Trump’s second term to resemble his first.
“I just do not feel like it has gotten a lot better,” she said.
Kristen Slaven, 41, a Mississippi mental health therapist who typically votes Republican, also said the country had not moved in the right direction.
“It definitely doesn’t feel like we have trended in the right direction,” Slaven said. “Obviously wars don’t help. When they’re necessary, I understand. But our focus on renaming bodies of water and pieces of land, that’s just stupid to me when people can't feed their family.”
Tariffs, Iran war add to economic concerns
Trump’s economic difficulties extend to his trade policy. Only about three in 10 Americans approve of his handling of trade negotiations with other countries, down from about four in 10 in March.
Meanwhile, 64% said Trump had “gone too far” with new tariffs, compared with 58% in January.
Americans also remain broadly unhappy with the war with Iran. About 69% said the war had not been worth fighting, up from 64% in July, while only 28% approved of Trump’s handling of Iran.
Despite the wider frustration, Republicans remain more likely than the broader public to attribute high prices to factors outside Trump’s control. About 67% of Republicans said external factors were more responsible for high prices.
Fred Naumann, 51, a Republican and longtime Trump supporter from Wisconsin, said inflation was difficult to address. He supports tariffs and the war with Iran, according to AP.
Overall, only about three in 10 Americans approve of Trump’s performance as president, while roughly six in 10 say the country is “much” or “somewhat” worse off than when he began his second term.
Border security remains one area where Trump retains relatively stronger support, with about half approving of his performance.
Trump faces more economic blame than Biden
Trump’s 26% economic approval rating is comparable with former President Joe Biden’s 28% rating in June 2022, when inflation had reached record levels during the Covid-19 pandemic.
However, Americans were less likely to blame Biden’s policies for high prices before the 2022 midterm elections. In October that year, 44% said Biden’s policies were responsible for high prices, while 55% blamed factors outside his control.
The comparison has also featured in views from Trump voters. Sanchez said Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war had directly affected the economy, while he viewed much of the economic disruption under Biden as stemming from the pandemic.
“I think he has a lot to do with it. This war in Iran, the tariffs that he’s placing on other countries, obviously are affecting us,” Sanchez said. “Those two things are things he’s been directly involved in that directly affect the economy.”
Separately, a Wall Street Journal poll cited by The Hill found Trump’s overall approval at 37%, the lowest for a president shortly before a midterm election in the Journal’s polling going back to George HW Bush.
60% of respondents in that poll said Trump’s economic policies had worsened the economy, while 25% said they had improved it.
The Journal poll, conducted from September 16 to 21 among 1,500 registered voters, had a margin of error of 2.5 percentage points.

articles.title: India ranks 38th in Global Innovation Index, digital services and venture capital power innovation gains - Dailyhunt
articles.summary: India ranks 38th in Global Innovation Index, digital services and venture capital power innovation gains  Dailyhunt
articles.full_text:
India ranked 38th in the Global Innovation Index 2026, retaining its position as the leading innovation economy among lower-middle-income countries.
The World Intellectual Property Organization's Global Innovation Index, which ranks 139 economies, placed India first in Central and Southern Asia and first among lower-middle-income economies. India recorded an overall score of 40.1.
India has also emerged as one of the fastest long-term climbers among middle-income countries. Along with China, Vietnam, Turkey, the Philippines, Morocco and Indonesia, The country has made some of the biggest advances in the index since 2013.
India ranked 49th globally on innovation inputs but 25th on outputs, highlighting its ability to translate a relatively modest innovation resource base into technology and commercial outcomes.
India ranked first globally in exports of information and communication technology services and fourth in late-stage venture capital deals.
However, the report also pointed to structural weaknesses that could make the next stage of India's innovation climb more difficult.
While India has one of the broadest innovation profiles among major middle-income economies, WIPO said it remains relatively weak in the number of researchers and scientific articles. Further gains would depend on expanding research, technology adoption and firm-level innovation beyond the country's dominant digital and startup sectors.
India among longest-standing innovation overperformers
India also remained an innovation "overperformer" for the 16th consecutive year, meaning that its innovation performance was higher than would normally be expected at its level of economic development.
India was also one of only two middle-income economies, along with China, classified as a global hub for both inward and outward greenfield R&D and high-tech investment.
India maintained four locations among the world's 100 largest innovation clusters.
Bengaluru ranked 25th globally, followed by Delhi at 27th, Mumbai at 43rd and Chennai at 79th. Mumbai climbed three places while Chennai gained five positions; Bengaluru fell four spots and Delhi slipped one.

Indian Railways has approved the 6 km Barbil-Bolanikhadan doubling project of South Eastern Railway at a completion cost of Rs. 1.22 bn. The work is intended to strengthen rail infrastructure on an important mineral movement corridor and support rising freight demand in the region.
The project will facilitate additional freight traffic of 8.9 MTPA on the section after commissioning and is expected to reduce delays affecting freight trains. The Barbil-Bolanikhadan route has been identified as part of Indian Railways’ Energy, Mineral and Cement Corridor, which is designed to support the movement of key industrial commodities.
The existing section is single-line and currently carries about 9 MTPA, including roughly six loaded rakes a day of originating iron ore traffic. The traffic consists entirely of high-grade ore and pellets transported from SAIL’s Bolani mines and private sidings operated by Rungta and Khatau Narbheram to major steel plants and ports.
The doubling work is planned ahead of the full realisation of SAIL’s mine expansion and additional port and plant capacity. It is intended to prevent capacity constraints on the designated mineral corridor as mining, industrial and port activities grow in the region.
The approved project will improve rail connectivity for iron ore shipments to steel plants and ports while increasing operational capacity on the route. Indian Railways said the work would support future freight requirements, strengthen the Energy, Mineral and Cement Corridor and enable smoother movement of cargo across the mineral-producing belt.

Kavach is an indigenously developed Automatic Train Protection (ATP) system designed to improve operational safety. The Finance Ministry has raised alarms over the upcoming Rabi season, citing potential yield disruptions due to a strong El Niño and ongoing global monetary policy headwinds. This warning comes on the heels of the IMD cutting the monsoon forecast to 90% of the long-period average, marking the fourth-lowest monsoon since 2001. Concurrently, the government has trimmed its crop-year foodgrain target by 2.63 million tonnes, indicating a highly cautious domestic outlook.
Market snapshot: The Indian macroeconomy faces a twin challenge of climate and monetary policy headwinds as the Ministry of Finance warns that a strong El Niño could disrupt upcoming Rabi crop yields and trigger upside inflation risks. This caution is echoed globally as Asia-Pacific stock indices trade mixed at the October 1 open, balancing softer U.S. PCE inflation data against persistently high government bond yields.
Data Snapshot
- India's government cut the foodgrain production target for the 2026-2027 crop year by 2.63 million tonnes to 373.93 million tonnes.
- The India Meteorological Department reported that the June-September 2026 monsoon ended at 90% of the long-period average, the fourth-lowest since 2001.
- PMFBY crop insurance enrollment surged by approximately 20% to 27.3 million farmers in Kharif 2026 due to heightened weather uncertainties.
What's Changed
- The government's crop-year foodgrain target has been revised downwards to 373.93 million tonnes, a drop of 2.63 million tonnes, from previous higher projections.
- The final Southwest monsoon performance of 2026 closed with a 10% deficit compared to the initial projections of a 92% to 94% average.
Key Takeaways
- Agricultural Vulnerability: The strong transition to El Niño presents immediate downside risks to soil moisture, threatening winter-sown Rabi crops like wheat, mustard, and pulses.
- Trimmed Production Goals: The proactive reduction of the foodgrain output target to 373.93 million tonnes reflects the government's focus on managing expectations and buffer stocks.
- Inflation Overhang: Deficient monsoon soil-moisture reserves combined with potential global policy tightening keep food and headline inflation risks elevated.
SAHI Perspective
From SAHI's analytical lens, the Finance Ministry's vocal concern about El Niño highlights the persistent sensitivity of India’s inflation path to seasonal weather patterns. While agricultural GVA contribution to GDP has moderated over decades, food prices remain the heaviest driver of the CPI basket. The tight reservoir levels and deficient September rains suggest that the RBI will likely maintain its hawkish stance or pause rate cuts, choosing to prioritize inflation control over growth stimulation in the near term.
Market Implications
The combination of agricultural deficits and high global bond yields represents a headwind for consumption-linked sectors. Expect some defensive rotation into sectors less reliant on rural demand, such as IT or Pharma, while FMCG, fertilizer, and tractor manufacturers could face margin pressures if rural income expectations soften.
Trading Signals
Market Bias: Bearish
Persistent monsoon deficit at 90% of LPA and a cut in the foodgrain output target by 2.63 million tonnes indicate rising inflation risks, which will likely delay monetary easing.

Trigger Factors:
- October reservoir water levels across major river basins
- Sowing updates for major Rabi crops like wheat and mustard in November
- Next RBI Monetary Policy Committee meeting in October 2026
Time Horizon: Near-term (0-3 months)
Industry Context
Indian agriculture heavily relies on the Southwest monsoon, which provides 70% of the country's annual rainfall. The IMD's confirmation of the 2026 monsoon being the fourth-lowest since 2001 poses a direct threat to rural liquidity. Historically, years with below-normal monsoons (such as 2023 at 95%) resulted in sharp volatility in vegetable and pulse prices, pushing up retail inflation and forcing policy interventions like export bans on key food commodities.
Key Risks to Watch
- Reservoir Depletion: Below-normal reservoir storage going into October directly limits the irrigation potential for water-intensive Rabi crops.
- Monetary Policy Transmission Lag: Continued high global yields limit the space for domestic rate cuts despite moderating core CPI.
- Rural Demand Slowdown: Lower crop yields could curb rural discretionary spending, hitting FMCG volume growth and tractor sales.
Recent Developments
In late September 2026, the IMD reported that the final Southwest monsoon ended with a 10% deficit, prompting the Ministry of Finance to direct insurance companies to accelerate PMFBY crop insurance enrollment, which has now touched 27.3 million farmers.
Closing Insight
A structurally resilient urban economy provides a strong buffer, but India's macroeconomic path cannot fully decouple from rural realities. Investors should maintain a defensive posture, monitoring October sowing statistics closely as a leading indicator of inflation trajectory and interest rate paths.
