articles.title: Disapproving nuns painted over the risqué frescoes in Rome's long-neglected Villa Silvestri Rivaldi for 3 - The Times of India
articles.summary: Disapproving nuns painted over the risqué frescoes in Rome's long-neglected Villa Silvestri Rivaldi for 3  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
For nearly three centuries, layers of plain paint and plaster hid a remarkable secret inside one of Rome’s long-neglected Renaissance villas. Now, restorers peeling back those layers are bringing colourful scenes of gods, goddesses, soldiers and mythological figures back into view, as per a report by Smithsonian Magazine.
The rediscovered artwork is inside Villa Silvestri Rivaldi, a sprawling 16th-century residence just a short distance from Rome’s Colosseum. The villa was acquired by Italy’s Lazio region for €25 million in 2024, and an extensive restoration is now revealing frescoes that had been deliberately covered after the property passed into the hands of a religious institution.
The murals include nude and semi-nude figures from non-Christian mythology, which reportedly offended the nuns who occupied the villa from the 17th century. The paintings were subsequently plastered over, leaving the Renaissance artwork hidden for around 300 years. Today, conservators are carefully removing those later layers using techniques including laser cleaning and water-based methods. In some sections, the process has already revealed entire scenes that had disappeared from view for generations.
Frescoes hidden behind plain walls
Its builder was Eurialo Silvestri, a chamberlain and close associate of Pope Paul III
Villa Silvestri Rivaldi was built between 1534 and 1547, when Rome was undergoing a major artistic and architectural transformation. 
Its builder was Eurialo Silvestri, a chamberlain and close associate of Pope Paul III, who hoped the grand residence would help strengthen his ambitions of becoming a cardinal.
Although that ambition did not succeed, the villa became home to a succession of prominent figures and families, including members of the Medici and Colonna dynasties. Alessandro de’ Medici, who later became Pope Leo XI, was among those associated with the property.
The villa was designed to reflect the wealth and status of its occupants. Its interiors featured elaborate decorations, coats of arms and mythological imagery, while its gardens once included a large nymphaeum with 12 fountains, shell mosaics, statues and orange trees.
Its location, overlooking parts of ancient Rome, also influenced the themes chosen by the artists. Classical mythology and ancient Roman imagery were particularly suited to a residence built amid the ruins and monuments of the city.
But the villa's artistic character changed dramatically after 1660, when it became the property of the Conservatory of the Mendicant Spinsters. The religious institution operated a girls’ school and orphanage there and remained associated with the building for about three centuries.
During that period, the nuns objected to the nude figures and other pagan imagery decorating the walls. Instead of allowing the controversial images to remain visible, the murals were covered. For centuries, the Renaissance paintings effectively disappeared behind the new surfaces.
A hidden Renaissance gallery re-emerges
The first serious attempts to uncover the paintings began more than two decades ago. Between 2002 and 2006, conservators carried out cleaning tests on parts of the walls after suspecting that older murals were hidden underneath.
Those tests confirmed that significant artwork remained beneath the overpainting. But restoration could not proceed at the time because the villa was still owned by a religious order that did not have the funds required for the work, according to Paola Mezzadri, a conservator and restorer involved in the project.
The situation changed after Lazio acquired the property in 2024.
Restoration work has now moved into a more substantial phase, with teams stabilising the deteriorating building while simultaneously investigating and cleaning its historic decoration. The wider restoration project has been described as a roughly $40-million effort, including the property acquisition and work intended to give the complex a new public life.
One of the most striking discoveries is in the Hall of Divinities. There, restorers have uncovered monumental figures of goddesses, depicted in vibrant oranges, yellows and greens. Some appear with flowing robes while others hold armour or weapons. The scenes offer a glimpse of the elaborate mythological decoration that once transformed the villa’s interiors.
Researchers believe Prospero Fontana may have been responsible for at least some of the paintings. Art historians have also linked the decoration to Perino del Vaga, an important artist of the period and a pupil of Raphael’s circle. Drawings preserved at the British Library have helped researchers investigate the possible connection between Fontana and the frescoes.
More paintings still waiting to be uncovered
 In the Hall of the Emperors, restorers are uncovering scenes showing soldiers, cavalry, battles and even a lion.
The Hall of Divinities is not the only part of the villa yielding surprises. In the Hall of the Emperors, restorers are uncovering scenes showing soldiers, cavalry, battles and even a lion. Portraits of Roman emperors, including Titus and Hadrian, have also emerged as layers covering the walls are removed. Another section, known as the Hall of Cupid and Psyche, has yet to be fully investigated.
The work is painstaking because restorers have to distinguish between layers of later paint and the original artwork without damaging the fragile frescoes underneath. Modern techniques, including lasers and water-based cleaning methods, are being used to remove the overpaint while limiting the use of chemicals.
The villa’s story also extends far beyond the Renaissance. After the nuns left around 1970, the complex went through several later uses and periods of neglect. It became a centre for community arts and political activism and was eventually occupied by squatters.
Restorers have even found 20th-century graffiti alongside the centuries-old frescoes, creating an unusual record of the building’s successive lives.
For now, there is no fixed date for the villa’s complete restoration or for its eventual public opening. Researchers say the scale of the work means discoveries are still being made as restoration progresses.
What was once hidden behind plain walls is slowly becoming visible again: a Renaissance gallery of mythological scenes that survived centuries of changing tastes, religious objections, neglect and abandonment.
And after roughly 300 years behind layers of paint and plaster, the figures that the nuns once wanted hidden are finally returning to the walls of Villa Silvestri Rivaldi.

articles.title: Spain and France Welcome UK, But Rejoining EU Faces Hurdles - India News Network
articles.summary: Spain and France Welcome UK, But Rejoining EU Faces Hurdles  India News Network
articles.full_text:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and French President Emmanuel Macron have expressed willingness to welcome the United Kingdom back into the European Union following Brexit. However, despite this apparent positivity, officials have cautioned that unwinding Brexit will entail significant costs and sacrifices that may not be acceptable to either side.
The speculation surrounding the UK's potential re-entry into the EU has intensified since new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested that he would discuss this possibility at an upcoming summit with European leaders. Macron, addressing the media, remarked, 'Welcome back,' while Sanchez stated that Spain would 'open its arms' to the UK.
Nonetheless, insiders suggest that the reality of rejoining the EU is fraught with complications. There is ongoing concern in Brussels regarding the UK's political stability, particularly given the recent rapid changes in leadership. If the UK were to seek re-entry, it would likely revive complex debates regarding past exemptions and agreements that may no longer be on the table.
Burnham articulated his plans to explore options for the UK’s relationship with the EU, including potential participation in the single market or a customs union. However, this interest has been tempered by concerns voiced by former Labour officials who highlight the substantial costs associated with rejoining. One source indicated that re-entering could impose an additional burden of approximately £5 billion per year, due to the need to renegotiate budget rebates established during Margaret Thatcher's tenure.
Another significant consideration is the UK's existing free trade agreements, particularly with countries like India, which may need to be renegotiated should the UK re-enter a customs union with the EU. Presently, both parties seem inclined to focus on more manageable discussions ahead of the summit, which will likely centre on less contentious topics like carbon markets and youth mobility.
Despite the cautious optimism from Spain and France, relationships between the EU and UK remain complicated. Previous discussions on critical legislative initiatives, including the EU’s 'Made in Europe' policy prioritising EU-produced goods, have led to disagreements. Furthermore, the EU's €150 billion defence loan programme, aimed at supporting military purchases, has also been a topic of contention, with talks on UK involvement having stalled last year.
As the upcoming summit approaches, the broader agenda will need to balance ambition with the current political landscape and lingering tensions from the Brexit process. For now, both Sanchez and Macron appear to be in a welcoming mood, but the path to reconciliation and re-entry remains fraught with uncertainty and potential setbacks.

articles.title: RBI may raise repo rate by 100 bps through H1 2027: BofA Securities - cfo.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.summary: RBI may raise repo rate by 100 bps through H1 2027: BofA Securities  cfo.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.full_text:
New Delhi [India], September 30 (ANI): The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) may raise interest rates by a total 100 basis points through the first half of 2027, with Bank of America (BofA) Securities bringing forward its forecast for the first rate hike to October from December.
In its latest India Viewpoint report, BofA Securities said it expects the RBI to raise the repo rate by 25 basis points at its October 7 monetary policy meeting. It expects another 75 basis points of hikes thereafter, taking the projected terminal rate to 6.25 per cent.
The brokerage had earlier forecast a total 50-basis-point increase.
BofA said the RBI has less reason to wait as domestic growth remains resilient, while inflation risks are becoming broader. It pointed to oil prices staying around USD 100-110 per barrel for most of September, along with rising risks of fuel price increases and food-related supply pressures.
The brokerage expects the RBI to deliver 50 basis points of rate hikes in the fourth quarter of 2026 and another 50 basis points in the first half of 2027.
It also expects the central bank to change its monetary policy stance in December.
BofA said strong economic growth is reducing the need for the RBI to maintain accommodative monetary conditions. Non-food credit growth stood at 17.8 per cent year-on-year in September, while investment demand is expected to remain healthy in the second quarter of FY27.
The report also flagged increasing inflation risks, saying food inflation is becoming more broad-based and wholesale inflation is increasingly spreading to other sectors. Tradables inflation rose to 5.9 per cent in August 2026, it said.
According to the report, the RBI could raise interest rates by more than 100 basis points if real GDP growth remains around 7 per cent and headline inflation stays close to 5.5 per cent.
In such a scenario, front-end rates could rise above 6.5 per cent, BofA said.
However, a major slowdown in economic growth could lead to fewer rate hikes or no hike, the report said. This could happen if growth falls below 7 per cent and moves towards 6 per cent on a forward-looking basis. (ANI)

Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday warned the West against escalating the war in Ukraine, saying Russia could use “all weapons” in its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad comes under attack.
Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow, Putin said Russia had no plans to attack any European country but would respond if it faced what he described as Western aggression. He specifically pointed to Kaliningrad, a Russian territory located between Nato members Poland and Lithuania.
“If it comes to direct attack against the Russian Federation, in this case on Kaliningrad and possibly some other territories, of course the issue of using all weapons in our country’s arsenal will inevitably and unavoidably emerge on the agenda. This is unavoidable,” Putin said.
“The drills in the Baltic Sea, following one another … Then the attempts to arrest our ships and vessels. All this is an escalation. And then we began to hear statements regarding the Kaliningrad region,” Putin said.
Putin says Ukraine strikes hitting Russian economy
Putin also acknowledged that Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries were hurting the country’s economy, saying they had cost Russia about 1% of its GDP, CNN reported.
Ukraine has stepped up long-range drone attacks on Russian territory, particularly targeting oil infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has described the strikes as “long-range sanctions” intended to cut Russia’s revenues and military capacity and push Moscow towards negotiations.
Putin said Ukrainian attacks had also damaged more than 100 Russian ships in the Black Sea.
Why is Kaliningrad strategically important?
Kaliningrad is a strategically important Russian territory surrounded by Nato members Poland and Lithuania. It is a heavily militarised Russian exclave, meaning it is separated from Russia’s main territory. Located between Poland and Lithuania on the Baltic Sea, the region has a population of about 1 million and covers an area slightly larger than the US state of Connecticut, Reuters reports.
The exclave gives Russia a key military position in the Baltic region, hosting air defence, missile and naval capabilities that can project power into parts of northern and central Europe.
But its location also makes it vulnerable. Surrounded by Nato territory on its landward sides and separated from mainland Russia, maintaining supply lines or reinforcing the region could become difficult during a conflict.
Tensions around Kaliningrad have grown since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, as Nato strengthened its eastern flank.

articles.title: When Israelis flew 4,000 km to rescue 100 plane-hijack hostages. Netanyahu lost a brother - India Today
articles.summary: When Israelis flew 4,000 km to rescue 100 plane-hijack hostages. Netanyahu lost a brother  India Today
articles.full_text:
Fifty years ago, Israeli commandos flew roughly 4,000 km to Uganda to rescue more than 100 hostages held after Palestinian and German terrorists hijacked an Air France flight. The daring Entebbe raid succeeded, but Benjamin Netanyahu's elder brother Yonatan, who led the assault, was killed.
"Like somebody amputated your arms and legs, and you're never going to be whole again," said Benjamin Netanyahu, describing the loss of his elder brother Yonatan 'Yoni' Netanyahu, the only Israeli commando killed during one of the most audacious hostage-rescue operations in aviation history. "It changed my life and steered it to its present course," Netanyahu told UK-based newspaper The Guardian in 2016, four decades after Israel's Entebbe raid of 1979.
When Yonatan Netanyahu was killed, Benjamin Netanyahu was 26 and living in the US. As news reached him in the US that his 30-year-old brother, leading Israeli commandos in the Entebbe hostage rescue, had been killed, Benjamin Netanyahu drove for seven agonising hours from Boston to Ithaca to tell his parents himself. His father initially smiled on seeing him, but then saw his face and understood, letting out what Netanyahu recalled as "a terrible cry like a wounded animal".
More than 100 hostages (predominantly Israeli and Jewish passengers) were rescued by the Israeli commandos. The passengers were on Air France Flight 139, which was hijacked by four Palestinian and German terrorists shortly after it left Athens on June 27, 1976.
The flight, travelling from Tel Aviv to Paris via Athens, was first forced to Benghazi in Libya and then to Entebbe airport near Kampala, the Ugandan capital. There, more gunmen joined the hijackers and forces of Ugandan President Idi Amin supported the hostage-takers.
The hijackers held the passengers and the flight crew at Entebbe for nearly a week and demanded the release of 53 prisoners held in Israel and several other countries. While non-Israeli and non-Jewish passengers were released, more than 100 people (mostly Israelis and Jews), along with the Air France crew and some others, remained captive.
Responding to the situation, Israel prepared for a high-risk evacuation response. On the night of July 3-4, four C-130 Hercules aircraft carrying Israeli commandos flew roughly 4,000 km to Uganda, landed at Entebbe, stormed the terminal and brought the hostages out in a daring overnight rescue. Yoni Netanyahu, commander of Israel's elite Sayeret Matkal assault force, was the only Israeli soldier killed in the daring operation. Later, the mission was renamed Operation Yonatan in his memory.
Fifty years later, Israel on Wednesday faced a major aviation scare as a flight with 174, mostly Israelis, headed from Dubai for Tel Aviv.
The Omani co-pilot of the flydubai flight attacked Indian Captain Smit Machchhar mid-air and, according to Israeli officials, apparently attempted to crash the aircraft. The plane plunged more than 14,000 feet before control was regained. Netanyahu, now Israel's prime minister, claimed the co-pilot had undergone "radical Islamist indoctrination".
Despite being attacked and wounded, Smit Machchhar managed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing passengers to overpower the attacker before two off-duty pilots who happened to be travelling on the same flight, landed the aircraft with over 170 onboard, safely in Saudi Arabia's Tabuk.
Netanyahu said the intervention had prevented what could have become a "9/11" type catastrophe.
Yes, the two incidents are fundamentally different. And, the flydubai incident on September 30 was not a conventional hijacking like Air France Flight 139 was. Investigators from multiple Middle Eastern nations are yet to establish the attacker's motive. But the flydubai incident has inevitably recalled Israel's long and bloody experience with threats to civilian aviation, of which the rescue in Entebbe was one of the most defining missions. It also changed the life of Netanyahu, now Israel's prime minister, and is confronting another threat in the skies.
Here's the story of the 1976 hijacking and the Entebbe rescue from the time when terrorists taking over aircraft was too common. Airport security looked little like it does today. This story has a mix of Palestinian and German terrorists, Idi Amin's Uganda, a black Mercedes used as a disguise, four Israeli Hercules aircraft flying through the night and an Israeli rescue plan so improbable that surprise was one of its greatest weapons.
WHEN HIJACKING A PASSENGER PLANE WAS TOO COMMON
To understand the Entebbe rescue mission, let's have a look at how commercial aviation operated in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Aircraft hijackings were so frequent that, according to American aviation historian Janet Bednarek, at their peak one occurred somewhere in the world on average about once every five days. In 1969 alone, there were 87 hijackings worldwide. Between 1968 and 1974, US airlines suffered 130 hijackings, according to Bednarek's 2002 piece in the Smithsonian Magazine.
Initially, many hijackers wanted money, asylum or simply to be flown somewhere else. But Palestinian militant groups hijacked planes to make them visible instruments of political pressure on the Jewish nation. In July 1968, members of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) hijacked an El Al flight travelling from Rome to Tel Aviv. In September 1970, the PFLP seized several aircraft in the Dawson's Field hijackings (in Jordan). In 1970, PFLP hijackers blew up three empty passenger planes at Dawson's Field.
It was in this age of "skyjacking" that Air France Flight 139 took off from Athens on June 27, 1976.
HOW DID AIR FRANCE FLIGHT 139 END UP 4,000 KM AWAY IN UGANDA
Flight 139 had originated in Tel Aviv and stopped at Athens on its way to Paris. Four hijackers boarded during the stop at Athens. Two were Palestinians associated with the PFLP's external operations and two were Germans, Wilfried Bose and Brigitte Kuhlmann, associated with the Revolutionary Cells, a West German far-left militant group active in the 1970s and 1980s. Soon after the Airbus A300 took off for Paris, the gunmen seized control.
Captain Michel Bacos later recalled that the hijacking took place only minutes after the departure. "The hijacking was carried out four minutes after the plane took off from Athens towards Paris," Bacos told Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronothin in an interview four decades later.
Bose entered the cockpit armed. "Every time I tried to look in a different direction, he pressed the barrel of his gun against my neck," Bacos recalled.
The aircraft was diverted to Benghazi (in Libya), where it remained for hours and refuelled. It then headed south towards Uganda.
At Entebbe on the banks of Lake Victoria, the hostages were moved into the airport's old terminal. More militants joined the original hijackers. Ugandan soldiers guarded the site, and the "Butcher of Uganda", Idi Amin, repeatedly appeared before the captives while publicly portraying himself as a mediator.
The terrorists demanded the release of 53 prisoners, 40 of them held by Israel and the others in West Germany, France, Switzerland and Kenya. They threatened to begin killing hostages if their demands were not met. Then came one of the most disturbing moments of the ordeal.
The captives were divided, with Israelis and some people identified as Jewish separated from most of the other passengers. Because two of the hijackers were German, the selection inevitably carried echoes of the Holocaust for some hostages. Accounts differ over precisely how the selection was conducted, but contemporary reporting confirms that Israeli passengers were separated while groups of other captives were released.
Four days after the hijacking, by July 1, most non-Israeli captives had been freed, leaving more than 100 hostages at Entebbe. Their deadline given by the hijackers was fast approaching.
HOW ISRAEL PLANNED A RESCUE 4,000 KM FROM HOME
Israel initially had no easy military option, with the hostages held nearly 4,000 km away in a foreign airport guarded by hijackers and Ugandan forces. Israel needed to fly a sizeable force across international airspace, land without alerting the hijackers and the Ugandans, find the correct terminal, kill the hostage-takers before they could execute their captives and then get everyone out.
Fuel was a major challenge. The Israeli aircraft needed enough range to fly thousands of kilometres, carry out the rescue and get the hostages out of Uganda. But Israel had an advantage. It knew Entebbe.
Israel and Uganda had once maintained close relations, and an Israeli construction company had built the old terminal, where the terrorists kept the Israeli and Jewish captives. Plans of the building could therefore be obtained. Israeli intelligence gathered information about the airport. The military planners worked through different rescue possibilities. The final plan was built around a surprise.
Four C-130 Hercules transporters would fly to Uganda. Commandos would land at Entebbe and race towards the terminal before the hijackers understood what was happening. The rescue plan also relied on an audacious deception trick.
A black Mercedes and Land Rovers were loaded aboard an aircraft. Once on the ground, Israeli troops would drive towards the terminal in vehicles intended to resemble Idi Amin's motorcade. The hope was that Ugandan guards would hesitate long enough for the Israelis to get close.

articles.summary: After Red Sea losses, Yemen’s government forces hold the line | Conflict News  Al JazeeraYemen’s Taiz on Verge of Liberation by Ansarullah Forces  تسنیمUS Iran War Live Updates: Yemeni army carries out 13 air strikes on Houthi positions in Taiz  The Times of IndiaDozens reportedly killed as Yemeni forces battle major Houthi offensive in Taiz  Arab NewsStrong explosions heard in Yemen capital: AFP journalist  Gulf News
articles.full_text:
Yemen’s Houthi rebels conducted intense attacks across frontlines in Taiz governorate on Thursday, as the Iran-allied group attempts to build on its lighting offensive that captured the country’s Red Sea coast last month.
Thus far, Yemeni government forces have been able to hold their positions on the frontlines and even claimed to have inflicted heavy losses against the Houthis.

- list 3 of 3‘We no longer eat three meals’: Yemen’s displaced face daily fight for food
Still, there are few signs that the Saudi-backed government intends to begin a serious counteroffensive against the Houthis in the near future, despite the head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council Rashad al-Alimi calling for a general mobilisation against the rebels on September 25.
The government instead seems to be pursuing a more gradual process, building up its military forces and attempting to make them more cohesive.
Abdul Basir al-Bahr, a senior official with the internationally recognised government army’s Taiz Military Axis, told Al Jazeera that the general mobilisation call was part of that effort.
Al-Bahr said plans include bringing reserve personnel back into the military’s ranks and retraining them, alongside local anti-Houthi fighters and civilian volunteers.
He stressed that the measures were at an early stage and their battlefield impact could not be judged yet.
In Taiz, Al Jazeera’s field monitoring has found that fighting has continued since early September without any major shifts that can be directly attributed to the general mobilisation.
The picture is similar on other fronts, including the Kahboub Mountains overlooking the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, and in Lahj, south of Taiz.
Yemeni government field commanders told Al Jazeera the general mobilisation had not yet led to frontline reinforcements.
But that does not mean that military activity has not intensified. On Monday, Colonel Majid al-Nazili, spokesman for the government’s military forces, said the forces had carried out more than 400 strikes over a 24-hour period against the Houthis, causing losses in personnel and equipment.
Advances stall
The ability of the Yemeni government’s military to halt further Houthi advances since the Red Sea reversal appears to reflect a combination of more favourable defensive terrain in the Taiz mountains and Lahj, as well as increased firepower.
The loss of the coastline was aided by weak coordination among anti-Houthi forces, who – despite officially being under one military chain of command – appeared divided and unable to respond quickly to the Houthi advance.
In both Taiz and Lahj – as well as Marib in Yemen’s north – anti-Houthi forces have shown more unity and have years of experience preventing Houthi military advances. Government-aligned forces have also had time to reinforce areas where the Houthis are attempting to advance.
The use of air power is also growing, with government forces reporting hundreds of air, drone, artillery and other strikes targeting Houthi positions and reinforcements in the past few days.
After having seized stretches of the Red Sea coast, the Houthis now need control of the mountainous high ground overlooking Bab al-Mandeb and the roads leading inland to consolidate those gains. Their attempts to take that high ground have so far failed, while the expanded territory has increased the manpower and logistical burden of defending their new positions.
The result, so far, is increasingly a battle over roads and supply lines, with neither side so far able to reproduce the kind of rapid breakthrough seen on the Red Sea coast.
Al Jazeera’s Yemen Editor, Ahmed al-Shalafi, said that the current Houthi attack on Taiz was the result of the group’s desire to secure its coastal gains, as well as an attempt to separate government forces.
He attributed their lack of success so far to a number of reasons.
“When you are talking about Taiz, you’re not just talking about Taiz itself, Taiz is connected to Lahj, Aden, Hodeidah, it has political importance, geographical importance, military importance,” al-Shalafi said.
“There is a difference between the Houthis entering Mocha and between them entering Taiz [city],” he added. “Firstly, the front is strong, there is a cohesion between the tribes and the local forces and the government forces … Secondly, the Houthis do not have a strong base of support in Taiz.”
